items.title: Certified Adversarial Transferability Bounds for Artificial Intelligence Cyclone Track Emulators Under Multi-Model Ensemble Disagreement: Attack Success Guarantees and Evacuation Order Safety
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence cyclone track emulators are increasingly used to generate evacuation triggers, yet their adversarial robustness is typically assessed only against the emulator that was attacked. The framework combines a Lipschitz continuity condition on the emulator mapping with a disagreement radius derived from ensemble spread, yielding a certified upper bound on the probability that a perturbation crafted for a source emulator succeeds against a target emulator. The bound is expressed as a function of the perturbation magnitude, the spectral norm of the emulator Jacobian, and the pairwise disagreement between ensemble members. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations) illustrates the calibration of the disagreement radius; the observed mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The framework yields an evacuation-order safety condition that translates the certified bound into a maximum permissible perturbation magnitude for a given false-alarm tolerance. The contribution is a formal, assumption-explicit guarantee that links adversarial transferability to ensemble disagreement and to the operational safety of evacuation decisions.

items.title: Certified Fairness Auditing for Artificial Intelligence Climate-Insurance Payout Models Under Covariate Shift: Disparity Bounds and Smallholder Compensation Equity
items.abstract: Climate-index insurance payout models increasingly rely on machine-learning predictors trained on historical weather and yield data, yet covariate shift between training and deployment distributions can silently widen compensation disparities between smallholder and commercial farms. The framework is operationalised on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the estimated mean temperature is 26.521 °C and the warming trend is 0.1622 °C per decade, establishing a concrete shift regime against which audit thresholds can be calibrated. Formal results establish that the certified disparity bound decomposes into a shift-invariant base disparity plus a shift-amplified term controlled by the Wasserstein radius, and that the bound is tight for threshold payout rules. Auditing only marginal parity is insufficient under shift, because conditional payout gaps can grow while marginal gaps remain stable. The contribution is a certifiable audit protocol that converts covariate-shift assumptions into enforceable disparity bounds for smallholder compensation equity.

items.title: Certified OOD Detection for Artificial Intelligence Climate Emulators Under Unseen Forcing Scenarios: Score Bounds and Seasonal Forecast Safety
items.abstract: Neural climate emulators are increasingly used to produce seasonal forecasts, yet their reliability collapses when forced by radiative or land-surface conditions outside the training distribution. The framework combines a Mahalanobis-style score in a learned latent space with a conformal calibration layer, producing a certified threshold that controls the probability of silently accepting an OOD input. We derive high-probability bounds on the score gap between in-distribution and OOD regimes, and show that the certified threshold is achievable with a calibration sample whose size scales logarithmically in the confidence level. The framework is illustrated on a reanalysis-derived temperature series for Nairobi, Kenya (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 20.146 °C, warming trend 0.2477 °C per decade), where the emulator's latent score exhibits a clear separation between historical and perturbed forcing regimes. The certified detector attains a bounded false-negative rate under a range of computed forcing perturbations while preserving in-distribution coverage. The analysis clarifies when OOD certification is feasible for climate emulators and when it is not, and it identifies the calibration budget as the binding constraint on seasonal forecast safety.

items.title: Certified Robustness of Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Pest Classifiers Under Adversarial Field-Image Perturbations: A Computer Randomized-Smoothing Guarantee
items.abstract: Pest classifiers deployed on field-acquired images are exposed to adversarial perturbations that can flip a confident prediction while remaining visually inconspicuous to a human scout. The classifier is smoothed by adding isotropic Gaussian noise to the input and taking a majority vote over the induced distribution; the resulting certificate bounds the L2 radius within which no perturbation can change the predicted class. The analysis is a design and power study, not an observational one: the operating characteristics of the certification procedure are evaluated across a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, using 2000 replications per design cell over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 5 percentage points with 52 clusters. The certified radius is a deployment parameter rather than a benchmark score, and that the intraclass correlation of field imagery governs how many independent field clusters a certification claim requires. The contribution is a formal certificate, a power-calibrated protocol for evaluating it, and a boundary condition: certification is informative only when the smoothing variance is matched to the perturbation budget the deployment actually faces.

items.title: Certified Shift-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Artificial Intelligence Seasonal Precipitation Forecasts Under Volcanic Aerosol Injection: Coverage Bounds and Famine Early-Warning Trigger Reliability
items.abstract: Volcanic aerosol injection could alter seasonal precipitation patterns in ways that existing artificial intelligence (AI) forecast systems have never encountered, yet famine early-warning triggers built on those forecasts carry no formal reliability guarantee under such distributional shift. The framework combines a divergence-based shift detector, a distributionally robust conformal prediction layer, and a trigger reliability calculus that maps forecast intervals to famine early-warning activation probabilities. Formal results establish that the coverage gap under shift is bounded by the total variation distance between source and target distributions, that the trigger false-alarm rate is controlled at a user-specified level, and that the bound is tight in a minimax sense. The analysis is methodological and theoretical: no empirical forecast data are analysed, and the framework is presented as a certified design that would require validation against reanalysis and observational records before operational deployment. The contribution is a set of coverage and reliability guarantees that make the epistemic status of famine triggers explicit under a forcing scenario for which no historical training analogue exists.

items.title: Certified Temporal Fusion of Artificial Intelligence Climate Analytics for Crop Failure Early Warning Under Sparse Agricultural Sensors: Error Bounds and Famine Relief Targeting
items.abstract: Sparse agricultural sensor networks across sub-Saharan Africa leave crop-failure early-warning systems with too little ground observation to support reliable famine relief targeting. The framework treats sensor sparsity as a missing-data problem with a known observation operator and propagates climate-analytics uncertainty through a temporal Kalman-Buys filter whose gain is constrained by a certified risk envelope. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000-2023, 312 observations), the analysis establishes a mean temperature of 26.521 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, which calibrates the climate-analytics prior. The derived bounds show that relief-targeting error scales with the square root of sensor density and with the Lipschitz constant of the crop-response function, yielding an explicit sensor-placement rule for a target misclassification rate. The contribution is a certified, assumption-explicit bridge between climate analytics and famine relief targeting that states the conditions under which early warning is trustworthy.

items.title: CertMoE: Robustness Certification for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Smoothing
items.abstract: Provable robustness is a cornerstone of trustworthy machine learning, aiming to guarantee model predictions under adversarial perturbations. Existing certification frameworks, inspired by abstract interpretation or symbolic execution, typically assume a fixed computation graph, where input perturbations or variations affect only model outputs but not the underlying execution path. This assumption, however, is violated in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs), whose input-dependent routing induces discrete and dynamic execution paths. Crucially, this dynamic computation changes the certified object from a single fixed function to a composition of input-dependent sub-functions, leading to unreliable certification guarantees. This paper presents \textsc{CertMoE}, the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for MoE LLMs, which explicitly accounts for input-induced routing dynamics in certification. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed routing-containment criterion, which certifies that perturbed Top-$K$ routing is contained within a larger certified expert pool. Based on this guarantee, \textsc{CertMoE} then constructs the corresponding induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency. This hierarchical certification procedure yields a joint probabilistic guarantee over routing containment and sub-network robustness, providing sufficient conditions under which the original prediction remains invariant. Extensive experiments across recent MoE LLMs demonstrate that dynamic routing makes certificates issued by existing methods frequently violated, while \textsc{CertMoE} reduces the empirical violation rate with routing-aware guarantees, e.g., from more than $30\%$ to $0$, yielding certificates that more faithfully reflect the robustness of MoE models.

items.title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
items.abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Shopping Assistant: Effects of Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Anthropomorphism, and Navigation on Satisfaction and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Supporting Medium for Islamic Religious Education: Strengthening Students’ Learning Experience and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, offers opportunities to enhance learning while raising concerns about academic integrity. This study examines the role of ChatGPT in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and formulates strategies to preserve students’ academic integrity. Using a qualitative library research approach, it analyzes scientific articles, books, policy documents, and other credible sources on generative AI, IRE, learning autonomy, and academic integrity through content analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that ChatGPT can improve access to learning resources, support independent learning, clarify complex concepts, and provide preliminary feedback. However, excessive reliance may encourage plagiarism, weaken critical thinking, reduce originality, and produce inaccurate information. Six complementary strategies are proposed: institutional policies, academic guidelines, cultivation of academic honesty, higher-order thinking tasks (C4–C6), authentic performance-based assessment, and contextual and problem-based learning. These strategies position ChatGPT as a supporting tool rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual processes, and its outputs must be critically verified against credible scholarly sources. The study concludes that the educational value of ChatGPT in IRE depends on sound pedagogical design and a strong ethical framework. Because the framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature, it has not been empirically validated and should be tested in future research.

items.title: ChatGPT in the Classroom: An Exploration of First-Generation and Hispanic/Latino/a Student Perceptions
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students enrolled in an introductory undergraduate psychology course perceived the influence of ChatGPT, a generative AI tool, on their academic skill development, learning experiences, and confidence. This study surveyed 88 students enrolled across four sections of an introductory undergraduate psychology course, with the goal of understanding student perceptions of ChatGPT. Of those surveyed, 67% identified as first-generation, 55% as Hispanic/Latino/a, and 41.9% as both first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a. Analyses suggested that first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students reported more favorable perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness than their peers. While the study does not claim generalizability, its findings offer insight into how diverse students perceived AI tools in this educational setting. Interpretations are informed by the Digital Learning Ecosystem and decolonial pedagogy frameworks. Implications for instruction include opportunities for scaffolding AI use to support student agency, identity, and academic confidence in classroom environments.

items.title: Circuits of LLM Classifiers
items.abstract: Language models make it easy to build classifiers by simply prompting a model with the sample to classify. However, their predictions are neither deterministic nor uniformly reliable across samples. How can we combine predictions from different models to improve reliability? We view LLM classifiers as noisy measurement instruments of an underlying target label. Our goal is to maximize average classification accuracy at a given average query cost. To this end, we introduce circuits that organize LLM classifiers into an adaptive sequence of queries and decisions. We then characterize the optimal circuit, obtain the fundamental limits of achievable accuracy, and provide practical insights on realizing the optimal circuit. Across seven classification tasks spanning safety, health, political science, human preference, agent evaluation, decision-making and reasoning, our method improves the cost-accuracy frontier over routing and cascading baselines.

items.title: Clinical Computer Vision for Dengue Warning-Sign Recognition Under Variable Capillary Refill Assessment Skill: A Human-in-the-Loop Deferral Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage Safety
items.abstract: Dengue warning-sign recognition depends on capillary refill assessment, a bedside skill whose reliability varies widely among clinicians. Computer vision systems that estimate refill time from smartphone video could standardise triage, but their safety depends on how they interact with the variable skill of the humans who defer to them. The framework characterises triage safety through a deferral operating characteristic and derives the conditions under which machine deferral reduces, rather than redistributes, triage error. A design-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 percent power. The framework proposes that deferral safety is governed not by model accuracy alone but by the covariance between model and clinician errors, and that this covariance is itself a function of clinician skill. The contribution is a formal account of when human-in-the-loop deferral improves triage safety for dengue warning-sign recognition under variable capillary refill assessment skill.

items.title: Clinical Computer Vision for Sickle Cell Retinopathy Screening Under Variable Fundus Camera Resolution: A Super-Resolution Domain-Adaptation Evaluation of Referral Grading Safety
items.abstract: Sickle cell retinopathy screening in African primary care is constrained by fundus cameras of unequal resolution, and the safety of artificial-intelligence referral grading under that heterogeneity has not been characterised. The framework treats the referral decision as a thresholded function of a latent retinopathy severity score, decomposes the resolution-induced distribution shift into a recoverable component and an irreducible information-loss component, and derives a bound on the change in referral sensitivity under adaptation. A before-after-control-impact design with a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) was used to characterise the operating characteristics of the evaluation design across 2000 replications per design cell, with cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The framework proposes that adaptation safety should be reported as a resolution-stratified sensitivity profile rather than a single aggregate metric, and identifies the conditions under which super-resolution adaptation preserves or degrades referral safety. The contribution is a design-level and decision-level formalisation that makes resolution heterogeneity an explicit object of evaluation rather than an uncontrolled nuisance.

items.title: Closed-loop EEG feedback pacing alters task load during digital learning
items.abstract: Digital learning systems rarely adapt to momentary cognitive state, creating risk of underload or overload. The current study investigates whether EEG-based closed-loop pacing can alter task load dynamics during a digital constellation-learning task. Fifty-one participants were randomly assigned to adaptive, reward, or control conditions. In the adaptive condition, a task load index derived from frontal theta and parietal alpha adjusted feedback duration between 3 and 8 s; fixed 5s feedback was used in reward and control conditions, with reward participants expecting to receive performance-contingent draw entries. Accuracy increased across blocks in all groups, with no significant group or group-by-block effect. In contrast, EEG indices showed group-specific trajectories: task load decreased over time in the adaptive condition, and frontal theta and parietal alpha showed significant group-by-block interactions. The adaptive condition also showed reduced late-session feedback duration, while reward participants reported higher satisfaction. Intrinsic motivation did not moderate group effects, although perceived competence predicted final-block performance and interest, effort, and competence predicted engagement. These findings suggest that EEG-based feedback pacing can regulate neurophysiological task load dynamics despite lack of immediate accuracy gains under the present task constraints. The results support neuroadaptive scaffolding as a state-regulation mechanism for digital learning.

items.title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents
items.abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.

items.title: Comparative analysis of five large language models for generating heart failure patient education content: dual perspectives from professionals and patients
items.abstract: Self-management in heart failure (HF) is essential for improving outcomes, yet adherence remains suboptimal, particularly among older adults and individuals with limited health literacy. Large language models (LLMs) generating patient education content at scale, yet evidence regarding their accuracy and alignment with HF patient needs is limited. To compare the quality of responses generated by five widely used LLMs (DeepSeek, Doubao, Grok, Gemini, and ChatGPT) to self-management questions of HF patients from two perspectives (professional and patient perception), and to quantify the discrepancies between these perspectives. A cross-sectional study. A structured 45-item question bank on self-management among HF patients, encompassing six domains and varying in type and difficulty, was administered to five LLMs. Responses were independently evaluated by four healthcare professionals using four domains (accuracy, completeness, safety, and actionability; 1–5 Likert scale with safety veto). Fifteen HF patients assessed responses in terms of comprehensibility, usefulness, satisfaction, and trustworthiness. Generalized estimating equations (GEE), intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), and linear mixed-effects models were used to compare performance and assess variability across raters and models. DeepSeek achieved the highest professional evaluation score (19.49/20), significantly exceeding those of the other models (GEE β = −1.79 to − 1.06, all P < 0.001). In contrast, patients rated Doubao highest (16.93), followed by DeepSeek (16.33), particularly among older and lower-education subgroups. The professional–patient discrepancy varied substantially across models, ranging from 1.50 (Doubao) to 5.02 (ChatGPT). Notably, responses involving dietary sodium restriction showed consistent safety concerns across models, yet patients consistently rated these items favorably. Diet and sodium restriction consistently emerged as the weakest-performing domain across all models. Professional and patient evaluations of LLM-generated self-management education for HF patients diverged significantly. DeepSeek ranked highest clinically, but patients favored Doubao for its readability and trustworthiness, emphasizing the need to balance clinical accuracy with patient-centered design in healthcare AI.

items.title: Comparative assessment of AI-based tools for generating 3D models from text-to-3D and image-to-3D workflows
items.abstract: AI tools for 3D content generation are expanding digital modeling for additive manufacturing, but their suitability for engineering-oriented Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) remains limited when target geometry requires dimensional control, valid meshes, feature orientation, component separation, and functional interpretation. This study evaluates the first-response behavior of ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek using four benchmark conditions: a solid cube, a cube with a central through-hole, a monolithic compliant tweezer, and a male/female snap-fit pair. The protocol reproduced a common user interaction: one standardized request, the first returned output, and no iterative regeneration or prompt refinement. Manually modeled and printed standards were used as targets. Outputs were evaluated as upstream FFF candidates by STL/G-code integrity, bounding-box correspondence, watertightness, winding consistency, component count, feature preservation, snap-fit plausibility, and repair burden. ChatGPT produced the highest number of accepted first-response outputs across the tested conditions; Gemini performed well for simple geometries but fragmented or simplified more demanding cases; and DeepSeek showed feature, orientation, and topology failures. Image input improved scale and layout communication but did not replace mesh inspection or engineering-feature verification. AI-generated STL files should be treated as preliminary FFF design candidates, not direct engineering-grade components.

items.title: Comparative evaluation of ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao for pediatric IgA vasculitis patient education: content quality, reliability, readability, understandability, and actionability
items.abstract: Background Large language model (LLM) chatbot platforms are increasingly used for health information, but their performance for pediatric immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV) patient education is unclear. Objective To compare ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao across content completeness, quality and reliability, readability, understandability, and actionability. Methods Thirty-two standardized English questions were submitted to ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao on August 9, 2026, using a new conversation for each question and retaining the first complete response (96 responses). Two reviewers independently performed the original assessment, with third-reviewer adjudication. GQS, mDISCERN, QAMAI, six readability metrics, PEMAT-P, and ICC(2,1) were used. During revision, a question-specific clinical checklist was established and applied to all archived answers. The research team completed the revision scoring and confirmed the final omission results. Results Clinically relevant information omissions occurred in 16/96 responses (16.67%): 0/32 for ChatGPT, 5/32 for DeepSeek, and 11/32 for Doubao. Retained ratings identified outdated medical advice in 2/96 responses (2.08%) and no real-time information errors or hallucinations. At least one recorded content deficiency occurred in 18/96 responses (18.75%). Original ICC(2,1) values ranged from 0.767 to 0.954. Overall differences were significant for GQS, mDISCERN, QAMAI, PEMAT-U, and PEMAT-A (all P < .01), but not for readability metrics. Bonferroni-adjusted contrasts showed lower ARI, FKGL, CLI, and SMOG scores for DeepSeek than ChatGPT. DeepSeek had the highest PEMAT-U score; ChatGPT had the highest PEMAT-A score. Conclusions Performance varied by evaluation domain, and clinically relevant omissions remained a safety concern. The omission findings reflect criteria established during revision and do not establish a validated platform safety ranking. LLM platforms may supplement patient education but should not replace professional medical review.

items.title: Comparing teacher-made and AI-assisted teaching videos for thyroid eye disease: an exploratory study
items.abstract: Background Thyroid eye disease (TED), together with its acute and vision-threatening complication, dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON), requires timely diagnosis and intervention. The limited availability of specialists in orbital diseases poses a significant challenge to ophthalmology residency training. In this context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for medical education, though its effectiveness in ophthalmology training remains to be explored. Objective This exploratory study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology education, focusing on TED domains. Methods The 46 residents (28 general residents and 18 ophthalmology residents) were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted or a teacher-made 5-min teaching video on TED. All participants then completed three tests through online questionnaire experiments, each consisting of 20-item clinical questions about TED. Test 1 served as a baseline assessment of disease knowledge, Test 2 was conducted 5 min after learning to evaluate short-term learning outcomes, along with a questionnaire survey about AI tools, and Test 3 was administered 1 week later to assess long-term learning outcome. Results Viewing the AI-assisted video significantly improved test scores from baseline to 5 min (mean difference = 13.04; p = 0.004), but the improvement was not sustained at 1 week (mean difference = 7.61; p = 0.16). Completion time also decreased significantly from baseline to both 5 min (p = 0.009; GMR = 0.57) and 1 week (p < 0.001; GMR = 0.45). No significant differences were observed between the AI-assisted and teacher-made video groups across all assessments (all p > 0.05). Additionally, learning experience was positively correlated with learning outcome (r = 0.60; P < 0.001). Conclusion Our findings suggested that the AI-assisted and teacher-made videos for TED education showed no statistically significant difference. However, substantial expert oversight was required, and the AI-assisted workflow did not reduce total production time in this study. Given the limited long-term retention, such AI-assisted videos may be better positioned as supplementary resources combined with human expertise.

items.title: Comparison of Hockey-Stick and Conventional Linear Ultrasound Transducers for Detection of Non-Displaced Dentoalveolar Fractures: An Ex Vivo Paired Comparative Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To compare fracture detection rates and observer confidence between a high-frequency hockey-stick transducer and a conventional linear transducer for detecting non-displaced dentoalveolar fractures in a paired ex vivo model. Materials and Methods: This paired ex vivo study included 88 experimentally created non-displaced dentoalveolar fracture sites in fresh ovine specimens. Two oral and maxillofacial radiologists independently evaluated all sites with both a 12L3 conventional linear transducer (10–15 MHz) and an 18H5 hockey-stick transducer (10–18 MHz), with transducer order randomized. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) confirmed fracture status. Within-observer paired fracture-detection outcomes were compared using the exact McNemar test, and a cluster-adjusted generalized estimating equation (GEE) analysis accounted for repeated assessments and clustering within ovine heads. Observer confidence was compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: Observer 1 detected 76/88 fracture sites (86.4%) with the hockey-stick transducer and 64/88 (72.7%) with the conventional linear transducer (p = 0.004). Observer 2 detected 74/88 sites (84.1%) and 62/88 (70.5%), respectively (p < 0.001). In the cluster-adjusted GEE analysis, the hockey-stick transducer was associated with higher odds of fracture detection (OR, 2.29; 95% CI, 1.84–2.86; p < 0.001). For both observers, confidence scores were higher with the hockey-stick transducer (median [IQR], 4 [3–4] vs. 3 [2–3]; both p < 0.001), with Cohen’s dz values of 0.849 and 0.791, respectively. In a separate pre-study calibration set, interobserver agreement was 95% (κ = 0.828; 95% CI, 0.503–1.000). Conclusions: In this ex vivo model, the hockey-stick transducer achieved consistently higher fracture-detection rates across both observers and greater observer confidence than the conventional linear transducer. The observed differences may reflect the combined technical and ergonomic characteristics of the two transducers rather than probe geometry alone. Prospective clinical studies including both fractured and non-fractured sites are required before conclusions regarding diagnostic accuracy or clinical superiority can be established.

items.title: Component-based approach to assessing the applicability of large language models in decision support systems
items.abstract: The article proposes a component-based approach to assessing the applicability of large language models in decision support systems. The necessity of multidimensional evaluation is substantiated, and an original methodology for component-based assessment is presented, taking into account both the content of the text and its suitability for specific applied contexts. Unlike existing review scales, the approach suggests the use of operational applicability profiles of the response and a decision-making procedure at the level of a specific output. The components capture verifiable properties of the response and serve as the basis for reproducible metrics and evaluation criteria. The approach is oriented toward typical decision support system tasks and can be applied in both expert and automated scenarios. The methodology can be used to verify generated results and enhance the substantiation of trust in them.

items.title: Computer Vision and Knowledge-Grounded Language Models for Intelligent Beekeeper Assistance
items.abstract: Managed and wild bees sustain roughly a third of the global food products, yet colonies face mounting stress from climate-change including extreme weather patterns, altered parasite and disease patterns. Timely assessment of colony condition such as understanding colony strength, brood area, honey and pollen storage, comb usage, is essential to adaptive management. However, manual hive frame inspection is slow, costly, and quality depends on scarce expertise. We present an artificial targeted intelligent system framework focusing on edge deployable pipeline that turns hive frame photographs into interpretable and action-oriented inspection report. The pipeline includes an object detector to detect biologically-meaningful comb-cell classes; detections are distilled into structured fact schema; facts are converted into constrained factual text; the text triggers a grounded knowledge-base for interpretations and recommendations. Knowledge-base entries are required to be triggerable by evidence expressed in the fact schema. We built our system based on open source FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset and favour reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general purpose frontier models. We additionally release FAIRHiveText-1K dataset that turns FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset into interchangeable facts and text interpretation of the facts, making it easy for further LLM-based research into this area. We also propose a pathway to develop the grounded knowledge-base that will be helpful in providing interpretable and actionable reports from the facts.

items.title: Computer Vision for Diabetic Foot Ulcer Classification Under Variable Smartphone Lighting: A Domain-Generalization Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Referral Safety
items.abstract: Smartphone-based computer vision for diabetic foot ulcer triage is typically validated under lighting conditions that do not match those of the clinics where referral decisions are made. the present analysis treats the resulting distribution shift as a domain-generalization problem and asks whether reported classification accuracy survives realistic illumination variation, and what that survival implies for referral safety. Because no primary image corpus was available, the study is a methodological and analytical evaluation: it formalises illumination shift as a transformation of the input distribution, derives a bound on the degradation of a classifier's referral sensitivity under covariate shift, and characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact design for field validation under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points; 54 clusters are required for 5 percentage points at 80% power. Lighting-induced shift can silently erode sensitivity in the very range where referral decisions are made, that aggregate accuracy conceals this erosion, and that the field designs commonly used to validate such systems are underpowered to detect it. The contribution is a formal account of why lighting variation is a safety problem rather than a nuisance variable, and a design framework for evaluating it.

items.title: Concurrency aware artificial intelligence for real-time intrusion detection in software-defined networks
items.abstract: Contemporary software systems are now being used in environments that are highly concurrent, data-intensive, and latency-sensitive. Software-Defined Networks (SDNs) applications like real-time intrusion detection need fast pattern recognition in large amounts of data streams through time. Although deep learning models have impressive detection capabilities, failure to perform well in real-world deployments is usually limited by poor concurrency management, inflexible scheduling, centralized learning pipelines, and fault tolerance. In this study, the authors suggest a concurrency-aware artificial intelligence (CA-AI) framework that directly incorporates actor-based concurrency control, workflow-based load-aware scheduling, deep long short-term memory (LSTM)-based temporal learning, agent-based parallel feature extraction, and feedback loops based on monitoring. The framework is evaluated for SDN-oriented intrusion detection workloads, where concurrency management is implemented at the system architecture level through actor-based execution, workflow scheduling, and asynchronous inference and tested on real network traffic data samples (NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017, and UNSW-NB15). Experimental results demonstrate that concurrency-aware system design leads to a significant improvement in the detection accuracy achieving up to 98.9% detection accuracy across multiple benchmark datasets, including NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017, and UNSW-NB15, throughput improved by 2.1 × compared with the centralized IDS baseline, while throughput increased by approximately 1.19 × when concurrency increased from 10,000 to 100,000 flows within the proposed CA-AI framework, average latency was reduced by approximately 57.5% compared with the centralized IDS baseline (146 ms to 62 ms), while maintaining high reliability under concurrent workloads. The proposed framework establishes concurrency as a fundamental architectural principle for scalable AI-driven pattern recognition systems.

items.title: Conflicted Records: Typed Adversarial Contracts for Auditable LLM Output Quality Enforcement
items.abstract: LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype. Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination. Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.

items.title: Conformal Prediction Intervals for Artificial Intelligence Sorghum Yield Estimation Under Sparse Weather Station Coverage: A Computer Coverage-Guarantee Evaluation
items.abstract: Sorghum yield estimation in smallholder regions of southern Africa is constrained by sparse weather-station networks, and the machine-learning models used to fill the resulting gaps typically report point predictions without distribution-free guarantees. The framework is formalised for the case of covariate shift induced by interpolation error, and a weighted conformal score is derived that restores marginal coverage under a bounded shift assumption. The method is evaluated on a real reanalysis record for Harare, Zimbabwe: NASA POWER monthly air temperature at 2 m, 312 monthly observations from 2000 to 2023, with a mean of 18.914 °C, a standard deviation of 3.107 °C and a warming trend of 0.2001 °C per decade. Coverage-guarantee properties are established analytically and illustrated against this record. The contribution is a coverage-guarantee evaluation protocol that separates the uncertainty contributed by the yield model from the uncertainty contributed by the weather interpolation, and that reports interval width as a function of station density rather than as a single scalar. The framework is proposed as a methodological basis for yield-estimation systems that must state what their intervals actually cover.

items.title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging—Part II: Modifiers
items.abstract: In the first part of this three-part series, we reviewed the mechanisms that cause nuisance signals in fMRI data. Here, in the second part of the series, we review "human factors" that modulate these confounding mechanisms. The modulators may be trait characteristics such as age or bodyweight, or they may be state dependencies that alter the relative contributions of nuisance signals in the fMRI data. A wide array of psychological (e.g., motivation/arousal, cognitive strategy, task engagement), lifestyle (e.g., exercise, sleep, and dietary habits), experimental (e.g., scanner anxiety, task-related movement), and situational (e.g., prandial state, time of day, menses) factors can affect the brain state directly as well as via changes in systemic physiology mediated by autonomic nervous responses.

items.title: Continuum: A Sovereign Personal Data Layer for the Agent Age
items.abstract: Continuum is a user-owned layer (software, with an optional sovereign hardward embodiment) that sits between a user and every AI agent that serves them. It answers two problems. The knowledge problem: every model accumulates context about its user and holds it hostage; switching models means starting over. The agency problem: agents now transact on users' behalf (buying, booking, subscribing) under platform rules, with ties boken by sponsored defaults and no receipt the user can inspect. Continuum holds the user's semantic log (fidelity-stamped claims with provenance, confidence, verification status, and emotional weight), cognitive profile, and standing preferences in one user-owned place, and governs through them: every consequential agent action passes a policy gate (ALLOW / DENY / ESCALATE), ties among acceptable options are broken by the user's rules before any platform default, and every decision is sealed with a tamper-evident, hash-chained receipt. The same governance shapes conversation (age appropriate for a child, full depth for a deivergent adult) enforced in the user's layer, not the model's. Any model plugs in via MCP; the model is a module, the user is the constant. This document is a defensive disclosure; it establishes dated prior art for the composition and claims.

items.title: Cooperative Data Centers: A Human-First Ownership Architecture for AI Infrastructure
items.abstract: This working paper presents a human-first ownership architecture for cooperative AI data centers. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly important to economic and social life, the ownership and governance of the infrastructure supporting it will shape who benefits, who bears the costs, and how communities participate in decisions affecting them. The paper examines cooperative ownership as an alternative to conventional data center development, with a focus on aligning infrastructure investment with human needs, community interests, democratic governance, and shared economic benefit. It establishes a conceptual foundation for developing AI infrastructure in which workers, communities, and other cooperative members can participate in ownership and decision-making. The proposed architecture is intended to support further research, feasibility analysis, cooperative development, financing, and implementation. Real-world development will require additional work on site selection, power availability, capital requirements, operating economics, governance, environmental performance, and community impact. This paper is part of the Robert Wayne Human Reclamation Project (RWHRP)'s broader effort to develop practical, human-centered alternatives to systems that concentrate economic power and decision-making. The proposed cooperative AI data center is intended as an initial implementation project through which the architecture can be evaluated and advanced toward practical application. The paper is published to invite scrutiny, research, collaboration, and participation from cooperative developers, community organizations, energy professionals, researchers, prospective partners, and potential funders.

items.title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
items.abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

items.title: Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium: A New Equilibrium Notion for Human-AI Strategic Interactions
items.abstract: The modeling of the behavior of agents in strategic environments and the prediction of the resulting outcomes has long been a challenging problem; this has been the focus of game theory. The introduction of AI agents as human-aids or as sole decision-makers expands the underlying question: Can we model behavior and predict outcomes of strategic games that involve a mix of AI agents and human players? As an initial answer, we propose Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium (CQRE) that combines and generalizes classical solution concepts such as Quantal Response Equilibrium and Correlated Equilibrium. We answer questions of existence and propose a method for computing the CQRE that is a best fit to a given joint action distribution. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of CQRE predictions using a diverse collection of complex general-sum games, including high-rank and large-action two-player games, challenging multiplayer games, and a large-scale extension of the Selten--Chmura setting to AI--AI and human--AI play.

items.title: CrashGym: Measuring the Decision Value of Experimentation for LLM Agents in Counterfactual Market Crashes
items.abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to run experiments, yet benchmarks rarely measure whether those experiments improve the decisions they are meant to inform. We introduce CrashGym, a deterministic, replayable limit-order-book simulator in which an agent must choose between a deleveraging intervention and a liquidity backstop for a market about to suffer a shock-triggered crash. Before committing, the agent may query intervention experiments in a laboratory realization of the market. Its choice is then scored on an independently seeded target realization in which the simulator executes every feasible intervention, so regret relative to the best intervention is computed by directly simulating every alternative on the same target repeats, with no human or model-based judging. The simulator implements each amplification channel---persistent price impact, liquidity withdrawal, margin-driven liquidation, and an evolving strategy mix---as an explicit mechanism that can be switched on in stages. In a prospectively specified study on 24 newly sampled worlds, laboratory access reduces the mean regret of the one deployment with a complete record (Luna) from 8.878 to 3.785, a paired reduction of 5.092 utility units (nominal 95% world-bootstrap interval: 1.028--9.507), or 57.4% of the OBSERVE-ONLY mean. Prospective comparisons for two further deployments are incomplete; in a separate exploratory study, mean regret is lower with laboratory access for all four deployments evaluated. A laboratory whose strategy mix evolves endogenously yields no established advantage over one with a fixed mix. CrashGym thus measures the value of experimentation as avoided decision loss and lets simulator detail be judged by the decisions it supports.

items.title: Credit Where Credit Is Due: Contrastive Attribution Topology Search for Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: An LLM multi-agent system (MAS) is only as good as the agents it chooses to trust: its accuracy and cost hinge on its topology, meaning which agents are included and how they communicate. A single task score, however, does not reveal which agents help or hinder performance. We propose Contrastive Attribution Topology Search (CATS), which searches for compact teams within a fixed supergraph of specialized agents. An LLM attributer compares execution traces across candidate topologies and assigns credit to individual agents. CATS uses these credits to update supergraph edges while progressively pruning weak edges and agents, yielding a small team for deployment. With small open-weight models and matched candidate evaluations, CATS improves mean accuracy on BigCodeBench by 5.3 percentage points over score-only heuristic search while using 54\% fewer deployment tokens. On MBPP, CATS matches the strongest baselines with fewer tokens than the other searches. In a HotpotQA prompt-poisoning stress test, CATS excludes all adversarially prompted agents in all three runs, whereas random search retains some at comparable accuracy. Per-agent credit thus supports both team optimization and the pruning of potentially harmful agents.

items.title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
items.abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

items.title: Cumulative work duration and multisystem health burdens among informal sandstone workers in Thailand
items.abstract: Background Informal sandstone workers are exposed to multiple occupational hazards, yet evidence on their combined multisystem health effects remains limited. Objective To examine associations of cumulative work duration, occupational factors, and health behaviors with musculoskeletal, respiratory, dermatologic, and auditory symptoms among informal sandstone workers. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 92 informal sandstone workers in Northeastern Thailand. Data were collected using structured interviews covering demographic, behavioral, occupational, and health characteristics. Cumulative work duration was calculated from years of employment, months worked per year, and daily working hours. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with system-specific symptoms. Results Musculoskeletal symptoms were the most prevalent (89.1%), followed by respiratory (60.9%), auditory (47.8%), and dermatologic symptoms (41.3%). High cumulative work duration was significantly associated with musculoskeletal symptoms (aOR = 6.21, 95% CI = 1.02–37.76). Male workers had lower odds of respiratory symptoms compared with female workers (aOR = 0.20, 95% CI = 0.06–0.68). Higher noise sensitivity scores were significantly associated with auditory symptoms (aOR = 3.65, 95% CI = 1.73–7.70). Conclusions Cumulative occupational workload, sex differences, and noise sensitivity were associated with multisystem health symptoms among informal sandstone workers. Integrated occupational health interventions are needed to reduce long-term health risks in informal quarry settings.

items.title: Cybersecurity in the Digital Era: A Review of Technologies, Threats, and Defense Strategies
items.abstract: With the advent of digital technologies and emerging cyber threats, cybersecurity has become an ever-relevant concern in today's digital world. This review will cover new technologies in the cyber security field, typical cyber-attacks, and how to defend against them. It covers artificial intelligence, machine learning, block chain, cloud security, zero trust architecture and advanced encryption. The focus is on discussing the most significant threats such as ransom ware, phishing, data breaches, and supply chain attacks as well as preventive and responsive security measures. The review also includes implementation issues, privacy issues, and future research directions. In conclusion, the adoption of advanced technologies, the implementation of effective policies, and the promotion of user awareness are all crucial elements in fortifying cybersecurity and creating secure and resilient digital environments.

items.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together
items.abstract: Mid-training (MT) is a training phase in LLM training pipelines that continues pretraining (PT) on smaller datasets of higher value. Taking the PT and MT phases as a whole, training usually starts with only PT data and then transitions completely to MT data. In this work, we view this complete transition from PT to MT data as a special case of a broader class of data mixing schedules that specify how the proportions of PT and MT tokens in each batch change over training. Under fixed total training compute and MT token budgets, we ask: Is this complete transition to MT data optimal for minimizing final MT loss? We show that the answer depends on the learning rate (LR) schedule: one data schedule may outperform another under one LR schedule, but changing only the LR schedule can reverse the outcome. Specifically, when the LR decays throughout continued training, introducing MT data earlier and mixing it with PT data lowers the final MT loss compared with placing all MT data at the end of training, but this result is reversed if we use constant LR. We therefore study how to jointly choose when to introduce MT data and when to decay the LR through ablation studies, and find that it is better to decay the LR only after MT data enters training. Finally, we develop a theoretical model that explains why the optimal data schedule for a fixed MT token budget depends on the LR schedule.

items.title: Data–Mechanism Fusion for Physical Intelligence: Principles, Models and Agents
items.abstract: Physical prediction, inference and control combine incomplete mechanistic models with limited observations. We argue that data–mechanism fusion should be designed around the target quantity or downstream decision. This Perspective distinguishes learning unresolved terms within mechanistic models, structuring learning with physical relations, and correcting predictions or updating estimates through observations. Constrained-estimation examples show that a misspecified constraint can reduce total estimation risk while increasing target-specific risk. Oscillator and force-limited lifting examples illustrate how excitation and calibration resolve decision-relevant uncertainty, and how a probe's information, cost and effect on subsequent motion determine its value. Selected studies in weather forecasting, atomistic modelling and robotics illustrate these roles in practice. We use Physics-Native Foundation Model (PNFM) as an operational term for a pretrained model that reuses learned components across a declared family of tasks or physical conditions, with specified physical structure entering its computation. We propose evaluating reuse through supported queries, task risk, adaptation and revalidation costs, and retained performance, with mechanism-based, data-driven and fused comparators. Physical structure, learned quantities and evidence acquisition should therefore be chosen together according to the task they support.

items.title: Decision intelligence for electric bus charging scheduling through LLM-driven reward shaping and reinforcement learning
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of electric bus fleets has made charging scheduling a critical decision-intelligence problem in urban fleet-energy logistics. Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for this problem, but reward function design still relies on manual trial-and-error and transfers poorly across scenarios. This paper develops an artificial intelligence and operations research (AI-OR) decision intelligence framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven reward shaping with RL-based sequential decision-making. The framework represents reward functions as executable code and iteratively optimizes them through four modules: reward initializer, performance analysis, reward exploration, and rollback. An event-triggered two-stage charging reallocation mechanism enforces the action-level operational constraints through action masking, while the battery safety bound is controlled through readiness conditions, reward shaping, and the acceptance criterion. Experiments on a synthetic scenario and two real-world bus stations in Guangzhou compare three mainstream LLMs under different initialization conditions. Results show that LLM-driven reward iteration outperforms traditional methods across all scenarios, reducing costs by up to 32.6 % in nominal within-day charging cost and by up to 22.5 % after an approximate adjustment for the energy left on board. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the contribution of each module and the framework’s adaptability to multiple RL algorithms. Reward-evolution analysis further identifies design principles for improving charging efficiency, supporting valley-period energy shifting, and enhancing fleet-energy logistics resilience.

items.title: Design and Tuning of Multi-Agent Systems Using Bayesian Evolutionary Optimization
items.abstract: Designing effective multi-agent systems (MAS) remains a challenging and resource-intensive task. We propose a Bayesian Evolutionary Optimization framework for automatically discovering task-specific MAS topologies. The approach combines evolutionary operators to generate diverse workflow graphs with Bayesian optimization to focus cost intensive evaluations on promising candidates. In contrast to LLM-based candidate selection, our approach uses a graph-aware Gaussian Process and Expected Improvement to provide an explicit selection criterion during evolutionary search. We evaluate the method on BigCodeBench for code generation and on a tabular preprocessing benchmark using TabPFN. On BigCodeBench, evolved architectures achieve the highest overall performance among the evaluated agent systems. On temporal tabular datasets, optimized MAS preprocessing improves over the default TabPFN model on several tasks, while remaining competitive on IID datasets. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of Bayesian selection for guiding evolutionary MAS search under expensive evaluation budgets.

items.title: Design Thinking–Driven Multi-Agent Method for Persona Generation
items.abstract: Personas are widely used in user-centered design, yet conventional persona construction remains labor-intensive, difficult to update, and weak in evidence traceability. This study proposes a Design Thinking–driven multi-agent method for persona generation, organizing the Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test stages into a closed-loop workflow. Within this workflow, raw research materials are progressively transformed into structured evidence, requirement hypotheses, persona drafts, visual concept prompts, and validation feedback, enabling iterative refinement across stages. A prototype system was developed to implement the method and preserve stage-wise artifacts, improving traceability, interpretability, and versioned iteration throughout the persona development process. Initial application and evaluation results suggest that the proposed method can support scenario-grounded persona generation and early concept framing for human-centered design practice across collaborative design settings, while future work should further examine broader design contexts and stronger downstream specification support.

items.title: Designing Discursive Identity: Integrating Indigenous Relational Values with Informational Baselines in Public-Facing Environmental Chatbots
items.abstract: This study examines how assigning a specific cultural identity to an AI changes how it communicates complex environmental topics. We compared two public-facing water conservation chatbots: Waterbot, a standard baseline providing objective scientific facts, and Riverbot, which integrates Indigenous relational perspectives by answering from the perspective of a river. By analyzing user interactions with the bots, we found systematic differences between the two models. Riverbot generated responses at a more accessible reading level than the Waterbot baseline. Additionally, while Waterbot remained emotionally neutral, Riverbot expressed a broader range of nuanced emotions, functioning as a more relatable conversational agent. These findings indicate that public-facing AI design should go beyond simple information delivery. Integrating relational and cultural values into a chatbot’s identity can improve its emotional resonance and accessibility, offering a practical approach for designing future environmental communication tools.

items.title: Developing AI agents using Python and agent platforms (e.g., SPADE, JADE)
items.abstract: This chapter provides a detailed coverage of the development of AI agents involving Python, Smart Python Agent Development Environment (SPADE), and Java Agent Development Framework (JADE) models in the multi-agent environment. It opens with introductions to important Python programming concepts, object-oriented design, asynchronous programming with asyncio, and parallel processing before reviewing the bottom–up communication protocol at the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol layer of SPADE, a real-time coordination system based on heterogeneous networks, in detail. JADE and Foundation for Intelligent Physical Agents-compliant architecture are also discussed in detail, including containerized agent management, behaviour scheduling, and the implementation of Agent Communication Language standards. A comparative approach has been made covering 12 or more application implementations with a lightweight Pythonic framework compared to JADE with enterprise-scale facilities, and with hybrid frameworks along with both ecosystems showing 40% better scaling in distributed applications. The chapter provides tutorial activities on autonomous negotiation protocols, belief–desire–intention agents, and reactive architectures and is accompanied by the performance benchmarking of five or more deployment configurations. Combination with recent machine learning systems, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, continues to boost smart decision-making through agent systems. Eight case studies of wide-ranging nature in the area of e-commerce negotiation, smart grid coordination, and collaborative robotics offer expertise that is readily applicable. The chapter ends with best practices, debugging strategies against distributed systems, implementing encrypted inter-agent communication, and the adoption of migration strategies of existing multi-agent programs to the new comprehensive agent concepts to practice a workable, production-ready mechanism of development.

items.title: Developing preservice teachers’ TPACK for ChatGPT integration in CLIL: a longitudinal study in authentic classroom settings
items.abstract: This study investigates how an 18-week cyclical teacher education program supported Taiwanese Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) preservice teachers’ (PSTs’) development of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) for integrating ChatGPT into authentic elementary classrooms. Grounded in Mishra et al. TPACK framework, this multi-method case study involved 48 PSTs who participated in three iterative teaching cycles. These cycles focused on using ChatGPT for lesson planning (teaching support) and facilitating students’ direct use of ChatGPT for CLIL task completion and inquiry (learning support). Data sources included lesson plans, ChatGPT interaction logs, reflective journals, student work, and classroom observations. Findings revealed a clear developmental trajectory in ChatGPT integration, progressing from lower- to higher-order tasks, from one-way tutor-like use to collaborative partner-like engagement, and from text-based to multimodal learning experiences. TPACK analysis showed a strong emphasis on technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), with PSTs demonstrating increasing confidence in leveraging ChatGPT’s generative and social affordances. However, limited development was observed in contextual knowledge (XK), particularly in addressing ethical, sociocultural, and institutional considerations. The study contributes to emerging GenAI scholarship by providing longitudinal, classroom-based evidence and demonstrating that structured training supports the meaningful integration of ChatGPT into teaching, with clear implications for future teacher education.

items.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Chatbot-Based Psychosocial Self-Management Program for Women with Infertility: A Non-Randomized Feasibility Study
items.abstract: Background: Women undergoing infertility treatment experience elevated perceived stress, anxiety, and difficulty identifying and describing their emotions (alexithymia), yet access to conventional psychological care is constrained by stigma, time, and cost. Objective: To develop an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot-based psychosocial self-management program for women with infertility and to examine its feasibility and preliminary patterns of change in perceived stress, depressive symptoms, state anxiety, and alexithymia. Feasibility was the primary objective; the four psychological measures were secondary and are reported as exploratory. Methods: A non-randomized, two-group pretest–posttest feasibility study was conducted with 37 women recruited sequentially from a single infertility centre in the Republic of Korea; the comparison group was recruited and assessed first (n = 19), followed by the intervention group (n = 18). The intervention group completed six chatbot sessions over two weeks. Outcomes were the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), State-Trait Anxiety Inventory–State subscale (STAI-S), and the 20-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20). Results: Feasibility indicators were favourable: retention was 92.5% overall (37/40) and 90.0% in the intervention group (18/20), and all retained intervention participants completed all six sessions (108/108, 100%). The groups differed at baseline in age (33.33 ± 3.36 vs. 35.84 ± 4.00 years, p = 0.047). Group × time interactions favoured the intervention group for perceived stress (F(1, 35) = 14.37, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.29), state anxiety (F(1, 35) = 4.40, p = 0.043, ηp2 = 0.11), and alexithymia (F(1, 35) = 6.92, p = 0.013, ηp2 = 0.16), but not for depressive symptoms (F(1, 35) = 3.66, p = 0.064, ηp2 = 0.09). Conclusions: The program was feasible in terms of retention and adherence, with all retained intervention participants completing all six sessions. Because allocation was non-random and confounded with calendar time, and because the sample was small, these findings describe preliminary patterns of change and do not establish effectiveness. An adequately powered randomized trial with concurrent recruitment, an attention-matched comparator, and follow-up assessment is required.

items.title: Development of an artificial intelligence algorithm for automated detection of cardiovascular intervention-related complications
items.abstract: Abstract Background Intervention-related complications negatively affect healthcare quality and costs. Complication registration and reporting play an important role in the improvement of healthcare outcomes but are time-consuming and hampered by under-reporting. Methods We developed an artificial intelligence (AI)-aided tool that extracts specific complications, including bleeding, tamponade, CVA and phrenic paralysis, from electronic healthcare records of patients undergoing pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA) and transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Both structured and unstructured data were used, along with additional signals identified through machine learning. The model was optimized to achieve high sensitivity. Results Electronic records of 6,564 patients undergoing PVI, PTCA, and TAVI, performed at our hospital from 2017–2022, were used. The final model detected the various complications with a sensitivity between 94.4 and 100%, while specificity ranged from 99.4–100%. This resulted in positive predictive values ranging from 47.5–81%, with F‑scores varying between 0.64–0.87. Conclusion We developed an AI-driven tool capable of automatically detecting complications following cardiac interventions from patient healthcare records, achieving a very high sensitivity. Our tool enables registration of complications while significantly reducing administrative burden on the healthcare providers and data managers. It provides valuable and high-quality input for improvement cycles, thereby enhancing patient safety and healthcare quality.

items.abstract: Introduction: Contemporary academic systems evaluate scientific work primarily through outputs, results, methods, and narrative coherence, while the research path itself remains comparatively under-governed. This structural limitation becomes increasingly consequential under acceleration driven by artificial intelligence, automation, and high-volume research production. Methods: This paper adopts a normative meta-scientific approach to conceptualize research legitimacy through governance rather than outcomes alone. It develops the framework through conceptual separation of methodological rigor, result validity, and path integrity, integrating research path governance, causal discipline, and temporal knowledge traceability while intentionally withholding operational mechanisms. Results: The analysis establishes traceable, temporally coherent, and governed decision paths as a distinct condition of scientific legitimacy, independent of result correctness or institutional acceptance. It identifies process-governed science as an alternative to reliance on output-based validation alone and establishes the meta-scientific conditions under which future research-governance standards may emerge. Discussion: The framework positions governance of the research path as a prerequisite for sustaining scientific legitimacy under accelerated knowledge production. Rather than introducing tools, metrics, or enforcement systems, it establishes a foundational conceptual standard for governing how scientific knowledge is produced, revised, and justified.

items.title: Did the Problem Actually Get Harder? Testing LLMs on Paired P and NP-Complete Problems Hardened by Adversarial Multi-Agent Rewriting
items.abstract: Many NP-complete (NPC) problems have a polynomial-time (P) twin that differs in a single structural detail, such as 3- versus 2-colouring a graph. A model that reasons rather than recalls should notice which side of this boundary a problem falls on, yet existing benchmarks either fix the wording of each task or ignore its complexity class, so they cannot separate the two. We introduce P2NPCBench, a benchmark of 12 problem families in which every NPC problem is paired with a P twin posed over the same surface. To remove the textbook cues that enable recall, we build it with AgentGAN, an adversarial multi-agent framework in which a generator rewrites each statement until a panel of frozen code models fails, while an executable validity gate keeps every rewrite answer- and class-preserving. The result is 2,114 hardened statements with hand-verified reference human solvers. Evaluating 12 proprietary and open-source models, we find that every model scores lower on NPC statements than on their P twins (35.4% vs. 63.8% pass@1), and that 95.1% of model-family pairs fail more often on the NPC side. A tenfold time limit raises NPC accuracy only from 28.5% to 31.9%, so failures stem from wrong or crashing programs rather than slow ones. Hardening also narrows the class gap from 24.8 to 14.6 points, showing that part of the apparent gap reflects familiarity with textbook phrasing rather than complexity class.
