items.title: Differentiable Crop Model Calibration for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Yield Forecasting Under Unmeasured Canopy Stress: A Computer Identifiability Evaluation
items.abstract: Differentiable calibration of process-based crop models is increasingly proposed as a route to yield forecasting that can absorb the unmeasured canopy stress that statistical learners cannot see. The proposal rests on an identifiability assumption that has not been examined: that the gradient of a differentiable simulator with respect to stress parameters carries enough information to recover those parameters from the yield and phenology observations that are actually available. the present analysis treats that assumption as a formal object. A differentiable crop model is written as a parameter-to-observation map, and structural and practical identifiability of the canopy-stress block are analysed under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. A before-after-control-impact design is evaluated across 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per cell. The stress block is structurally identifiable only when the observation operator contains a canopy-sensitive channel, and that under the declared variance structure 52 clusters are required for 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect. The contribution is a set of conditions under which differentiable calibration is informative rather than merely convergent, and a warning that low calibration loss is not evidence of recovered stress.

items.title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback
items.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient {model size $d$}. Such dependence is prohibitive in modern {overparameterized models} where $d$ is vast. In this work, we study \emph{Private Sparse RLHF} problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^* \ll d$ relevant features. We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings. Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_2$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + {s^*}^2/n^2\varepsilon^2)$ for $(\varepsilon,δ)$-Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + s^*/n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon$-Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP. Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

items.title: Differentially-Private Federated Learning for Computer Agriculture Pest Inference Across Smallholder Smartphone Fleets Under Cross-Device Heterogeneity: An Artificial Intelligence Privacy-Utility Bound
items.abstract: Federated learning promises to train pest-inference models on smallholder smartphone fleets without centralising raw imagery, but the differential-privacy noise required to protect individual contributions interacts with cross-device heterogeneity in ways that existing privacy-utility analyses do not capture. The analysis derives a closed-form expression for the excess risk of the privatised federated estimator as a function of the privacy budget, the number of participating devices, the local sample size, and a heterogeneity coefficient that quantifies the dispersion of device-level data distributions. The bound shows that the utility cost of privacy is not monotone in fleet size: beyond a threshold determined by the heterogeneity coefficient, adding devices increases the bias contribution faster than it reduces the variance contribution, so that privacy and heterogeneity compound rather than offset. A corollary establishes that clipping norm and noise scale must be co-tuned to the heterogeneity coefficient, and that the standard practice of fixing the clipping norm across devices is suboptimal when heterogeneity is high. The bound is stated for the convex smooth setting and its extension to the non-convex stochastic setting is discussed. The contribution is a device-heterogeneity-aware privacy-utility characterisation that reframes the design of differentially-private federated learning for agricultural pest inference as a joint tuning problem over privacy, fleet composition, and local data dispersion.

items.title: Digital Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Towards anEmirati Model for Protecting Family Identity and EnhancingSocial Cohesion
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), algorithmically curated platforms, and generative media are reshaping how people access information, communicate, and learn. These developments create educational opportunities while raising questions about privacy, misinformation, bias, family interaction, cultural identity, and social cohesion. This conceptual paper examines digital education as a framework for developing the knowledge, judgement, and ethical dispositions needed to participate responsibly in AI-mediated environments. It focuses on the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where national efforts to advance AI literacy provide a relevant policy context for considering how technological capability can be aligned with cultural context and human values. The paper uses a qualitative descriptive-analytical approach to examine selected international frameworks and institutional policy documents alongside conceptual literature on networked communication, media literacy, participatory culture, and digital ethics. It does not claim to measure the prevalence or causal effects of digital risks in Emirati families; rather, it synthesises relevant concepts and derives a proposed educational framework. The analysis identifies five mutually reinforcing pillars: digital national and cultural identity; media and algorithmic literacy; digital ethics and safety; partnership among families, schools, media, and public institutions; and a human-centred balance between technology use and face-to-face relationships. The paper argues that these pillars should be translated into age-appropriate learning outcomes, family guidance, teacher development, and coordinated institutional practice. It concludes that the proposed model is a conceptual contribution requiring subsequent expert review and empirical evaluation before its effectiveness can be established

items.title: Digital Media in Indonesian Language Learning: Teachers’ Practices, Students’ Responses, and Implementation Challenges
items.abstract: Digital technology has transformed Indonesian language learning in schools, but its classroom use depends on how teachers apply it, how students respond to it, and the obstacles schools face. This qualitative descriptive study examined teachers’ practices, students’ responses, and implementation challenges related to digital media in Indonesian language learning at the junior high school level. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with an Indonesian language teacher and open-ended questionnaires completed by 32 students and were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. Regarding teachers’ practices, the teacher integrated PowerPoint, instructional videos, Canva, Google Classroom, WhatsApp, laptops, projectors, and smartphones and selected them according to the characteristics of the material. Regarding students’ responses, students reported that digital media made the material easier to understand and increased their learning interest, activeness, intrinsic motivation, and confidence. Regarding implementation challenges, unstable internet connections, limited supporting devices, and uneven digital literacy hindered optimal use, which the teacher addressed by adapting media, limiting data-intensive applications, and rotating school devices. These findings suggest that teachers’ digital competence and school support for infrastructure and training are needed to optimize digital media in Indonesian language learning.

items.title: Digital Transformation of Risk Management in Infrastructure
items.abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping how infrastructure organizations identify, assess, and manage risk. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, the Internet of Things, and blockchain are transforming risk management from largely retrospective exercises into more forward-looking, data-rich, and continuously adaptive systems. In sustainability-driven infrastructure contexts, these tools offer earlier warning of physical and transition climate risks, more efficient resource and asset management, transparent supply chain monitoring, and closer alignment between operational decisions and long-term environmental, social, and governance objectives. This chapter examines the digital transformation of risk management through a sustainability lens. It begins with artificial intelligence and machine learning for predictive risk forecasting, including their application to climate risk, asset performance analysis, and project decision support. Digital twins are examined as dynamic representations of assets and systems that enable real-time monitoring, scenario simulation, and resilience planning. Internet of Things sensor networks are addressed as the continuous data infrastructure on which proactive risk detection and ESG monitoring depend. Blockchain is discussed as a mechanism for transparency and trust in complex infrastructure supply chains where sustainability assurance is structurally difficult. The chapter then addresses data ethics, governance, and algorithmic bias as substantive risk management responsibilities central to sustainability-driven practice. It concludes with practical considerations for selecting and integrating digital tools in infrastructure risk management contexts. Digitization does not remove judgment from risk management; it changes where and how that judgment is exercised, and it introduces new categories of risk that must be managed alongside those it helps to address.

items.title: Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (DistilBERT) for Multi-Class Mental Health Detection fromWeb-Scraped Reddit Posts
items.abstract: The increasing availability of social media data has created new opportunities for using artificial intelligence (AI) to study and support mental health awareness. This paper presents an offline machine learning framework that leverages natural language processing (NLP) to classify Reddit posts into distinct mental health categories based on linguistic patterns. The dataset was collected using the PRAW API from 26 subreddits on mental health, addiction, and control topics, yielding approximately 80,000 anonymized text samples. A pre-trained DistilBERT-base-uncased transformer model was fine-tuned for multi-class classification across eleven diagnostic categories, including anxiety, depression, stress, and addiction disorders. Texts were preprocessed through normalization, keyword filtering, and category mapping. Model training employed a weighted cross-entropy loss to mitigate class imbalance, with optimization performed using the AdamW algorithm in a fully offline Jupyter Notebook environment. The model achieved an overall accuracy of 77%, a macro-averaged F1 Score of 0.736, and a weighted F1 Score of 0.772. These results indicate that transformer-based NLP models can reliably distinguish between multiple forms of mental health discourse, demonstrating their potential as supportive tools for early detection or population-level analysis. The study underscores the importance of ethical data handling, transparency, and responsible AI design when applying language models to sensitive domains such as mental health.

items.title: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
items.abstract: Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types. Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector. We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target. AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers. It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus. Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings. A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.

items.title: District Hospital Trauma Survivor Mental Health Screening Text Message Reminder Timing and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Assessment Attendance in Zambian Clinics: A Randomised Evaluation of Nudge Schedules
items.abstract: District hospitals in Zambia discharge trauma survivors into a follow-up system that rarely reaches them, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) assessment attendance is the point at which the system most visibly fails. Text-message reminders are widely assumed to help, but the timing of those reminders has never been treated as a design parameter with its own behavioural logic. The framework distinguishes three timing dimensions: the interval between discharge and reminder, the interval between reminder and appointment, and the spacing of repeated reminders. It proposes that these dimensions operate through prospective memory, planning fallacy correction, and salience decay, and that their effects are likely to be non-monotonic. A worked design is presented for a three-arm randomised evaluation in which participants are allocated to a standard single reminder, a front-loaded schedule, or a spaced schedule, with attendance at PTSD assessment as the primary outcome. Reminder timing should be pre-specified as a schedule rather than a single send time, that the primary estimand should be attendance at the first scheduled assessment, and that the design should be powered to detect a difference of ten percentage points. The contribution is a transferable template for nudge-schedule evaluation in low-resource trauma care, not a report of trial findings.

items.title: Do You Feel Like Using GenAI? Scenario Emotional Valence Impact on Potential Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is becoming increasingly ubiquitous, creating questions about what factors are influencing its use. This study explored whether emotions in decision-making scenarios impact the use of genAI writing tools. We presented 35 writing-based scenarios, some associated with the six basic human emotions (sadness, anger, enjoyment, fear, surprise, disgust) and others created as neutral emotional conditions. College student participants were asked whether they would use a genAI tool to complete the task, and then to identify the emotion present. Most participants varied their decision to use AI tools. There were significant effects of emotion on the potential use of genAI assistance, with a higher intended adoption for fear and surprise contexts. Emotion strength also influenced potential AI use, with reported AI trust and task complexity increasing in stronger-rated scenarios. However, the overall rate of AI use was generally low. Implications for automation use and trust theories are discussed.

items.title: Does Code-Switching Disrupt Emotion Recognition? A Valence–Arousal Analysis of Affective Misalignment in Multilingual Human–AI Interaction
items.abstract: As multilingual communication increasingly involves code-switching, emotion recognition in mixed-language input has become a key challenge for human–AI interaction. This study examines emotion classification under English–Spanish and Spanish–English code-switching conditions using the valence–arousal framework. Five large language models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-5, Llama-3, Llama-4, and Claude Opus 4.7) were evaluated on 7,560 inputs across five code-switching ratios. Performance was assessed using accuracy, Macro-F1, and mixed-effects logistic regression, while errors were categorized as valence shifts, arousal shifts, or same-region confusions. Increasing code-switching produced a small but significant accuracy decline in both language directions. Under English-to-Spanish conditions, models generally preserved valence while showing greater arousal instability. Under Spanish-to-English conditions, GPT-5 showed increased valence-shift errors and was the only model with a significant direction–error-type association. Aggregate metrics can obscure distinct forms of affective misalignment. The proposed framework enables dimension-level comparison of error patterns across models, language directions, and code-switching ratios.

items.title: Does Every Instance Count Equally? Order Effects in LLM Multi-Instance Processing
items.abstract: Users increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to analyse collections of independent inputs, such as product reviews or social media posts, and return a single aggregated answer. This setting requires multi-instance processing (MIP), where a model combines information from multiple instances into one prediction. We study a task in which the model must infer a binary label for each instance, and identify the most frequent label among the full instance set. The correct answer should be invariant to instance order. By evaluating fifteen LLMs across five datasets and seven instance order patterns, with each instance set held fixed across patterns, we find substantial order sensitivity. Accuracy can differ by about 90 percentage points between the best and worst order patterns, with models generally more accurate when majority-label instances appear at the start than when they appear in the middle or at the end. For subsets of models, available reasoning traces and gradient-based attribution reveal uneven emphasis across positions. Traces disproportionately mention early instances, while attribution scores are generally higher near the beginning and end than in the middle. These results show that instance order can systematically bias aggregated predictions, highlighting the need to evaluate MIP across different input arrangements.

items.title: Does Generative Artificial Intelligence ( GAI ) Complement, Complicate, and Compromise Family Science Qualitative Analysis?
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines the relationship between generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools and interpretive qualitative research in family science. Drawing on existing literature and an illustrative analytic comparison, we compare human‐led coding, ChatGPT‐assisted coding, and ATLAS.ti‐assisted coding (with GAI built in). In conversation with the literature and our analytic comparison, we consider how GAI tools complement, complicate, and compromise meaning‐making processes central to interpretive qualitative family research. Considering both the literature and our comparison, we conclude that GAI can complement analysis by supporting organization, comparison, and early pattern recognition, but it also complicates and compromises analysis by shifting analytic labor from deep human engagement toward more rote prompt design, output verification, codebook cleanup, and documentation, dampening human insights, creativity, and judgment.

items.title: Dynamic thermal imaging for crop water stress detection across phenological stages: Enhancing irrigation scheduling precision
items.abstract: Thermal remote sensing and derived indices such as the crop water stress index (CWSI) can assess crop water status and support precision irrigation. However, most operational and artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches rely on fixed, season-long thresholds to interpret canopy–air temperature differences and often overlook the influence of crop phenology. This review synthesises evidence from grapevine, wheat, maize, potato and several other crops on how developmental stage affects the non-water-stressed baseline (NWSB), CWSI thresholds and irrigation-scheduling algorithms. It covers CWSI theory and estimation practices; crop-specific, phenology-dependent behaviour of baselines and thresholds; a comparison of threshold-based, machine learning, Internet of Things (IoT), digital twin and Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)-56 approaches with respect to crop phenology; and a conceptual framework for phenology-aware scheduling. Across the reviewed crops, baseline behaviour generally varied systematically across the growing season, the relationship between CWSI and crop water status generally strengthened after canopy closure and CWSI measured during reproductive stages was generally most closely related to yield. A quantitative audit of 56 AI-, thermal-imaging-, or CWSI-based studies found that 78.6 % either did not explicitly incorporate crop phenology or relied on day of year as a temporal proxy, whereas only 5.4 % explicitly encoded phenological stage. The proposed framework considers phenology explicitly in baseline estimation, threshold setting and data fusion or machine learning for irrigation scheduling; the framework will require multi-year, multi-site field validation before operational use. Future research should prioritise standardised phenology definitions and long-term, multi-location studies to establish and validate stage-specific parameters.

items.title: DynaWeave: Learning to Adapt through Dynamic Scenario Synthesis
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use tools to complete tasks in stateful environments. However, many training environments remain largely static apart from changes caused by the agent's own actions, whereas external events introduced by other users, services, or sudden contingencies in real environments can invalidate ongoing plans. To address this gap, we introduce DynaWeave, an automated synthesis framework that transforms existing static tasks into verifiable dynamic scenarios. The framework generates exogenous events relevant to each task, covering changes in task requirements, environment state, and external information. It uses directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to represent dependencies between events and an execution engine to activate them during agent interaction. A dynamic verifier revises only the evaluation checks affected by events that actually occur and retains all other checks. Using DynaWeave, we collect 2,095 verified interaction trajectories across 36 environments and use them for supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5 models. Experiments on Gaia2, CostBench, and ToolMaze show that DynaWeave achieves consistent improvements in overall performance across all three evaluated model sizes, increasing the task completion rate on CostBench by 67.34 percentage points and even exceeding the performance of Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview on ToolMaze. These results support dynamic scenario synthesis as a practical approach to training agents to adapt to changing environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/DynaWeave.

items.title: Early diagnosis program for multimodal primary open-angle glaucoma based on clinical process
items.abstract: Background Glaucoma is among the leading causes of blindness. It is important to detect glaucoma at early stages. Using structural and functional examinations to identify primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is critical. Computer-aided diagnosis of glaucoma requires multimodal data to identify an accurate and explainable model for early glaucoma diagnosis. Methods In this study, 301 multimodal data points were collected from the ophthalmology department at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University. Data regarding fundus photography (FP), retinal nerve fiber layer thickness (RNFLt), intraocular pressure (IOP) values, visual field examination parameters and age were obtained. A powerful deep learning network was used to segment the optic nerve head obtained from the FPs. Machine learning classifiers (MLCs) were adopted to obtain the final classification results using 3 datasets: early glaucoma eyes, suspected glaucoma eyes, and healthy eyes; moreover, the diagnostic results of glaucoma specialists and general nonglaucoma ophthalmologists were collected. Results The overall area under the curve was 0.9858. The accuracy values of the deep learning- machine learning system, the glaucoma specialist group, the general ophthalmologist group were 0.9478, 0.9493, 0.8725, respectively. Conclusions The algorithm delivers superior results in the early diagnosis of POAG. This study’s hybrid deep learning-machine learning framework can effectively assist with clinical decision-making for early POAG.

items.title: Effectiveness of a continuous ergonomic program on workplace health and cognitive strain in university employees
items.abstract: Background University staff are at high risk of musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) and mental workload due to prolonged static postures, poor ergonomic conditions, and high cognitive demands. These issues lead to significant health and productivity challenges, particularly in developing countries. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a participatory ergonomic intervention program on reducing MSDs and mental workload among university staff, and to enhance their awareness of ergonomic principles. Methods A quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-tests was used, involving 60 participants divided into control and intervention groups. The intervention included 8 weekly training sessions on ergonomics, workstation adjustments, and the introduction of ergonomic equipment. Data were collected using the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ) and NASA-TLX workload index, analyzed via paired t-tests and covariance analysis. Results The intervention significantly reduced mental workload by 24.17% (p = 0.008), with the highest reductions in physical (46.58%) and mental (35.84%) dimensions. MSDs prevalence decreased notably in the back (50%), neck (39%), and wrists (39–61.6%). The control group showed no significant changes. Conclusions Based on these results, continuous training and ergonomic adjustments are recommended, as they may help sustain the observed benefits over the long term. This approach has the potential to promote healthier work environments and could lead to enhanced productivity, although further longitudinal research is needed to directly confirm these broader implications.

items.title: Effectiveness of the Healthy Hearing Promoting Program (HHPP) among workers in large-scale industries: A randomized controlled trial in central Thailand
items.abstract: Background: Noise-induced hearing loss remains a significant occupational health concern in industrial settings. Adherence to protective behaviors among workers remains suboptimal, leaving them at continued risk of hearing impairment. Strengthening hearing health promotion is therefore essential. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of the Healthy Hearing Promoting Program in promoting noise hazard protection behavior and maintaining hearing capacity among workers in large-scale industries. Methods: This single-blind parallel-group randomized controlled trial included 66 industrial workers from two large-scale factories in central Thailand, randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 33) and a control group (n = 33). The control group continued routine occupational practices based on existing factory safety policies. Data were collected between December 2023 and July 2024. Noise hazard protection behavior was assessed at baseline, Week 10, and Week 14, while hearing capacity was evaluated at Week 34 (26 weeks after intervention completion). Statistical analyses were conducted using mixed-design ANOVA and Fisher's exact test. Results: There were no significant differences in baseline data between groups. The experimental group had significantly higher noise hazard protection behavior scores than the control group (F (1,64) = 41.67, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.394), with significant changes over time (F(2,128) = 48.02, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.429) and a significant group–time interaction (F(2,128) = 24.12, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.274). Between-group mean differences in protection behavior scores were 5.91 points (95% CI: 3.6, 8.2) at Week 10 and 7.39 points (95% CI: 5.3, 9.5) at Week 14. All participants in the experimental group demonstrated hearing thresholds within the normal range across all tested frequencies at follow-up. A small proportion of control group participants exhibited abnormal thresholds at frequencies between 500 and 4000 Hz. Conclusion: The program significantly improved noise hazard protection behaviors but no significant between-group differences in hearing capacity were demonstrated. The findings provide preliminary evidence to support occupational health nurses in developing and implementing theory-driven, multilevel hearing conservation interventions aimed at improving noise hazard protection behaviors among workers in large-scale industries. items.title: Effects of Passive Back-Support Exoskeletons on Postural Stability During Commercial Crabbing
items.abstract: Passive back-support exoskeletons may reduce low-back strain during physically demanding work, but their effects on balance in fishing environments remain unclear. This study examined how three passive back-support exoskeletons influenced postural stability during simulated commercial Dungeness crabbing tasks. Twenty-five healthy male participants completed pot handling and crab sorting under no-exoskeleton and exoskeleton conditions using Apex, Laevo, and Ottobock devices. Center-of-pressure (COP) and ground reaction force data were collected using force plates, and postural sway outcomes were compared within subjects. Results showed task-dependent effects. During pot handling, COP metrics were largely unchanged. During crab sorting, all three exoskeletons significantly increased anterior-posterior center of pressure mean velocity, with Apex producing the largest increase. Apex also increased medial-lateral mean velocity, suggesting modest reductions in stance control. Overall, passive back-support exoskeletons may be useful for selected crabbing tasks, but device selection, user training, and task-specific implementation are essential.

items.title: Emotional intelligence and self-disclosure strategies in WhatsApp profile photos among young adults
items.abstract: This study examines relationships among trait emotional intelligence (EI), self-disclosure (SD) dimensions and visual self-presentation in WhatsApp profile pictures among 186 Italian young adults. We investigated whether EI is associated with SD dimensions and whether visual characteristics relate to psychological traits using self-report measures and independent visual coding of profile pictures. The results show that trait EI is selectively correlated with the qualitative dimensions of SD (positive valence, accuracy and intentionality) but not with amount or depth, suggesting that higher perceived emotional competence is linked to more regulated, authentic and deliberate online communication rather than to greater frequency or intimacy of disclosure. Network analysis of visual parameters identified gaze direction and gaze engagement as the central organising elements of visual identity. Contrary to expectations, trait EI was not directly associated with visual self-presentation characteristics. However, SD depth and intentionality were linked to direct gaze and expressive facial displays, suggesting that deeper, more intentional SD involves a more engaged, deliberate visual presentation. These findings clarify how people manage digital identity on messaging platforms, informing HCI research on interface design, ergonomics, self-presentation and visual cues in computer-mediated communication.

items.title: Engagement or disengagement: understanding the emotional dynamics of EFL learners in GenAI-assisted writing from the sociocultural perspective
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL writing education, yet the emotional dimensions of student engagement in GenAI-assisted writing remain underexplored. This longitudinal multiple-case study investigates how Chinese EFL learners' emotional engagement evolves during a GenAI-assisted college writing course and what factors drive this evolution. Methods Drawing on the sociocultural framework of L2 student engagement with written feedback, we traced the emotional trajectories of three focal students across three writing tasks (exposition, group feature article, and argumentation) within a 14-week course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with stimulated recall, reflective reports, GenAI-student chatlogs, drafts, informal chats, and course syllabus, and analyzed via thematic analysis. Results Our findings reveal three qualitatively distinct trajectories: positive-resilient, characterized by sustained positive affect with temporary fluctuations; pragmatic-transformative, marked by a gradual shift from practical disengagement to critical engagement; and vulnerable-contingent, moving from moderate disengagement, through tentative peer-mediated improvement, to eventual breakdown and intensified disengagement. These trajectories were shaped by the dialectical interplay between individual factors (e.g., English proficiency, GenAI literacy, mindsets, beliefs, and emotion regulation) and environmental factors (GenAI-relevant task design, peer and teacher mediation, and institutional policies). Discussion The study extends the sociocultural framework by identifying English proficiency and GenAI literacy as critical developmental competencies, embedding GenAI-related factors across multiple environmental levels, and foregrounding emotional engagement as a dynamic, fluid state that interacts with behavioral and cognitive engagement over time. The findings challenge universalist claims about GenAI's uniform affective benefits and underscore the need for differentiated pedagogical approaches that attend to learners' diverse emotional needs in GenAI-mediated writing contexts.

items.title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution
items.abstract: Through a tangle of real-world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. Across nine frontier LLMs, solving and authoring prove to be distinct skills: the strongest solvers are not the strongest authors, while smaller models learn more from how others played and write the hardest environments and the most useful hints. Beyond the scores, the pairwise interactions form a microcosm of how models affect one another. Head-to-head outcomes are transitive and so yield a stable ranking; independent authors converge on the same designs; and in a reinforcement-learning study with Qwen3.8-27B, the learner's hint lift on an author's environments tracks how much training on those environments improves it on held-out reasoning and agentic benchmarks, whether the environments are its own or another model's. Each of these patterns has a counterpart in how models shape one another outside the duel. By staging these interactions under controlled conditions, Environment Duels offers a window onto how LLMs teach, challenge and learn from one another. Code is available at https://github.com/LLM-Duels/EnvDuels.

items.title: Environmental and systems‐based safety in the obstetric operating room: A narrative review
items.abstract: Abstract Cesarean delivery requires an operating room (OR) that supports maternal surgery and anesthesia while preparing for fetal‐to‐newborn transition and, when needed, concurrent maternal and neonatal resuscitation. This narrative review applies a human factors framework to noise, information displays, medication and equipment organization, layout, communication, ergonomics, and emergency preparedness. These factors are examined in relation to hearing the awake patient's concerns, recognizing maternal or fetal deterioration, accessing hemorrhage treatment, and coordinating newborn assessment without interrupting maternal care. Standardized layouts, structured communication, cognitive aids, and simulation may improve care processes, but evidence for their effects on maternal and neonatal morbidity varies, and some findings are extrapolated from non‐obstetric surgery. Environmental safety initiatives should therefore assess both the reliability of cesarean care and patient outcomes, including maternal morbidity, newborn thermal status, and the maternal birth experience.

items.title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

items.title: Ergonomic design of rock-climbing clothing: beyond static anthropometry to movement-informed design
items.abstract: Conventional garment design typically relies on static anthropometric measurements, which may not adequately account for changes in body dimensions and posture during highly dynamic activities such as rock climbing. This study investigates how climbing-specific movement analysis and dynamic anthropometry can inform ergonomic design of rock-climbing clothing. It combines a review of relevant research with observational and movement analysis of climbers using the Xsens motion-capture system to examine relationships between dynamic body dimensions and garment pattern requirements. The analysis identified changes in body dimensions during climbing and highlighted the crotch and inner-leg, knee, upper-back, armhole and sleeve regions as key areas for pattern development. The findings demonstrate the limitations of static anthropometry for dynamic garment design and indicate areas where pattern adaptations and ease require consideration. The study provides a basis for developing climbing-specific pattern-engineering strategies. Further prototype testing is required to validate specific modifications and ease allowances.

items.title: ERP and Accounting Information Systems in Higher Education: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: This study maps the research landscape on Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Accounting Information Systems (AIS) in higher education, covering both institutional implementation and the use of ERP/AIS as learning objects in accounting and information systems curricula. A scoping review was designed following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guideline. ScienceDirect, Scopus (through the Watase Uake platform), and Lens.org were searched for journal articles published between 2015 and 2026, which identified 390 records. After removing 86 duplicates, 304 unique records were screened on titles and abstracts by a single reviewer against predefined criteria, and 50 records were retained for the evidence map; no full-text screening or critical appraisal was undertaken. The retained records form four clusters: administrative ERP implementation and critical success factors (27 records), user acceptance and system success (11), ERP/AIS as learning objects (10), and emerging technologies including generative AI (2). Annual output was low and fluctuated between 1 and 7 records without a sustained upward trend. Among the 37 records naming a study context, the Middle East and South Asia were the most frequent (19 records) and Southeast Asia appeared in three; survey-based designs were the most common single design (17 of 50 records) but dominated only the user-acceptance cluster, and no abstract reports a longitudinal design. By placing the administrative-managerial and learning-pedagogical streams in one evidence map, this review identifies a fragmented field and highlights gaps in longitudinal evidence, graduate outcomes, and Southeast Asian contexts, including Indonesia.

items.title: Evaluation of Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Extension Consortia Under Ministry-Level Model Poisoning: A Governance Convergence Bound for Advisory Integrity
items.abstract: Ministry-level actors in agricultural extension consortia can poison the shared model that federated learning is meant to protect, and the governance question is not whether robust aggregation works in the abstract but what integrity guarantee a consortium can credibly promise its smallholders. The bound is derived analytically from the geometry of the robust aggregation rule and the political constraint that no single ministry may control more than a fixed share of update weight. Integrity is jointly produced by the statistical robustness of the aggregator and the institutional design of the consortium, and that neither alone suffices. Three governance levers follow: a participation cap calibrated to the aggregator's breakdown point, a public audit trigger tied to the bound, and a convergence criterion that treats advisory drift as a political as well as a statistical event. The contribution is a bridge between the machine-learning literature on Byzantine robustness and the political science literature on delegated authority in extension systems.

items.title: Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Pest-Surveillance Consortia Under Poisoned Extension-Device Reports: An Artificial Intelligence Governance Convergence Bound for Outbreak-Alert Reliability
items.abstract: Federated learning consortia that pool pest-surveillance reports from smallholder extension devices face a governance problem that is not captured by standard robust-aggregation theory: the adversary is not an anonymous network intruder but a ministry-level actor whose poisoning budget is set by administrative authority rather than by computational resources. The analysis is a replication-based design evaluation, not an observational study. Under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-four clusters were required for 80 per cent power at a 5-percentage-point effect. The governance convergence bound, not the statistical power curve alone, is the binding constraint on consortium design, and that the two must be evaluated jointly before an outbreak-alert system is certified.

items.title: Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated-Learning Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Cooperative Pest-Monitoring Under Adversarial Sensor Poisoning: An Artificial Intelligence Convergence-Guarantee Audit
items.abstract: Cooperative pest-monitoring networks that aggregate sensor evidence across farms through federated learning face a structural threat: a minority of compromised nodes can submit adversarial updates that survive averaging and corrupt the global model. Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are widely proposed as the remedy, yet their convergence guarantees rest on assumptions about update geometry that agricultural sensor deployments rarely satisfy. the present analysis audits those guarantees. It formalises the aggregation problem for a cooperative pest-monitoring federation, states the standard Byzantine-robust estimators (coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum), and derives the conditions under which each retains a bounded convergence rate under adversarial sensor poisoning. The audit shows that the guarantees are conditional on a contamination fraction and a heterogeneity bound that are not observable in deployment, and that the effective contamination fraction is inflated by non-IID pest phenology across farms. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) to show how many clusters a cooperative trial would need to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power: 52. Convergence-guarantee audits, not point accuracy comparisons, should govern the adoption of Byzantine-robust aggregation in computer agriculture.

items.title: Evaluation of Coalition-Formation Stability Bounds for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Advisory Councils Under Sequential Member Defection: A Governance Durability Estimation Strategy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence agriculture advisory councils are typically designed as standing coalitions of ministries, extension agencies, farmer organisations and technology providers, yet their durability under sequential member defection is rarely specified in advance. The analysis is a replication-based evaluation, not an observational study: no councils were observed and no defection events were recorded. Using a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design would require 52 clusters to detect a 5 percentage point defection effect at 80 per cent power. The before-after-control-impact estimator is a defensible durability bound only when the intraclass correlation is treated as a design parameter rather than a nuisance, and it specifies the conditions under which advisory council evaluations can distinguish genuine coalition stability from cluster-level heterogeneity.

items.title: Evaluation of Concept-Probe Sufficiency Audits for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Yield-Forecast Models Under Satellite-Revisit Sparsity: An Interpretability Reliability Bound for Smallholder Crop-Insurance Payouts
items.abstract: Concept-probe sufficiency audits are increasingly proposed as a precondition for deploying artificial intelligence yield-forecast models in smallholder crop-insurance, on the reasoning that a model whose internal representations can be decoded into agronomically meaningful concepts is safe to trust with payout decisions. The audit's inferential warrant is not intrinsic to the probe but depends on the temporal sampling regime of the satellite record that supplies the model's inputs. A formal reliability bound is derived for the sufficiency statistic under satellite-revisit sparsity, treating the probe's estimated concept alignment as a noisy measurement whose variance is inflated by the effective number of independent overpasses per growing season. The bound is then propagated to the payout decision through a before-after-control-impact estimator of the insurance indemnity, and the operating characteristics of that estimator are characterised under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The sufficiency audit's false-pass rate is governed jointly by revisit density and cluster count, that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80% power, and that the audit cannot by itself certify payout reliability below a revisit threshold that the bound makes explicit. The contribution is a reliability bound that converts an interpretability claim into a decision-theoretic one, together with the design conditions under which concept-probe sufficiency auditing is and is not a defensible gate for smallholder indemnity.

items.title: Evaluation of Concept-Probe Transfer Audits for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Cross-Regional Deployment: An Interpretability Generalization Bound for Smallholder Fungicide Safety
items.abstract: Concept-probe audits are increasingly proposed as a safeguard for computer-vision crop-disease classifiers deployed across regions, yet the audit's own transfer behaviour is rarely characterised. The audit is modelled as a two-stage procedure: a probe is fitted on source-region activations and then applied to target-region activations to certify that a safety-relevant concept, such as lesion evidence warranting fungicide application, remains decodable. A bound is derived that decomposes the target-region probe error into a source-region empirical term, a concept-distribution divergence term and a finite-sample concentration term. items.title: Evaluation of Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Computer Agriculture Land-Use Zoning Under Competing Tenure Claims: An Artificial Intelligence Pareto-Frontier Audit for Expropriation Risk
items.abstract: Agricultural land-use zoning in sub-Saharan Africa must reconcile competing tenure claims with productivity and equity objectives, yet the algorithms increasingly proposed for this task are evaluated almost exclusively on their ability to identify Pareto-efficient allocations. Pareto-frontier optimality is a necessary but insufficient criterion for zoning systems that allocate land under contested customary and statutory tenure, because a frontier can be efficient while systematically concentrating expropriation risk on politically marginal claimants. The framework is formalised as a constrained Markov decision process with a lexicographic constraint structure, and the audit is specified as a set of frontier-level diagnostics: constraint-violation density, risk concentration across tenure classes, and frontier stability under preference perturbation. No empirical data are analysed; the contribution is methodological and conceptual. The choice of constraint architecture, not the choice of learning algorithm, determines whether a zoning policy is tenure-safe, and that audits reporting only hypervolume or sparsity cannot distinguish tenure-safe from tenure-unsafe frontiers. The proposed audit provides a reproducible diagnostic that regulators can apply to any multi-objective zoning model before deployment.

items.title: Evaluation of Counterfactual Audit Sampling for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Procurement Under Bid-Rigging: A Governance Detection-Power Bound for Tender Integrity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly procured by agricultural ministries to allocate subsidies, score grant applications and forecast harvests, yet the audit designs meant to detect bid-rigging in those procurements have not been evaluated for their detection power. the present analysis treats counterfactual audit sampling as a governance instrument and derives a detection-power bound for the before-after-control-impact design that underlies it. The analysis is a replication-based evaluation of the estimator's operating characteristics under a declared variance structure: between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, residual standard deviation of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells defined by cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 52 clusters to reach 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect. At 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, power at that effect remained below the conventional threshold, and the minimum detectable effect at 80 per cent power fell only slowly as clusters were added. The bound implies that counterfactual audit sampling, as currently constituted, cannot certify tender integrity at the cluster counts African agricultural agencies can realistically audit. The contribution is a governance detection-power bound that reframes audit sampling as a statistical design problem rather than an administrative ritual.

items.title: Evaluation of Delegation-Chain Collusion Attacks on Liquid Democracy Voting for Computer Agriculture Cooperatives Under Quorum Thresholds: An Artificial Intelligence bribery-Resistance Bound for Participatory Governance
items.abstract: Liquid democracy lets members of computer agriculture cooperatives vote directly or delegate their weight to trusted peers, and it is increasingly proposed as a governance layer for participatory decisions on shared machinery, water and data. The delegation graph that makes this flexibility possible also creates a vulnerability that direct voting does not have: a colluding coalition can purchase delegations along a chain and concentrate voting weight without ever buying a single vote on the floor. the present analysis treats that vulnerability formally. It models a cooperative as a delegation graph with a quorum threshold, defines a delegation-chain collusion attack as a coalition that acquires consecutive delegations to route weight toward a target proposal, and derives a bribery-resistance bound that states the maximum share of the electorate a coalition must control before the quorum threshold can be met by purchased delegation alone. The bound is expressed in the coalition's size, the depth of the delegation chain, the quorum threshold and the cost of acquiring a delegation relative to the cost of acquiring a direct vote. Quorum thresholds interact non-monotonically with resistance: raising the quorum can either harden or soften the cooperative against chain collusion depending on whether the threshold is met by participation or by concentration.

items.title: Evaluation of Differential Privacy Budget Allocation for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Yield-Prediction Models Under Cooperative Data-Sharing Consortia: A Governance Privacy-Utility Bound for Smallholder Participation
items.abstract: Cooperative data-sharing consortia that pool smallholder yield records to train artificial intelligence (AI) prediction models face a governance problem that is not resolved by technical privacy guarantees alone: the allocation of a differential privacy budget across participating districts determines both the statistical utility of the resulting model and the distribution of privacy protection among members. The analysis is theoretical and methodological. It formalises the consortium as a federated learning arrangement in which a central curator allocates a total privacy budget across contributing units, and it derives the utility loss of the pooled yield predictor as a function of the per-unit budget, the number of contributing units, and the heterogeneity of yield distributions across units. The central result is a bound showing that equal per-unit budget allocation is utility-optimal only when units are homogeneous in sample size and yield variance; when they are not, equal allocation produces a privacy-utility frontier that is dominated by a size-weighted allocation rule. The paper further shows that the governance choice of allocation rule, not the choice of privacy mechanism, is the binding constraint on smallholder participation, because smallholders in heterogeneous districts face the largest utility penalty under equal allocation and therefore the strongest incentive to withdraw. The contribution is a governance privacy-utility bound that connects differential privacy budget allocation to participation incentives in cooperative agricultural data consortia, and a set of allocation principles that consortium designers can apply without access to the underlying data.

items.title: Evaluation of Differentially-Private Federated Distillation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Prediction Under Cross-Silo Heterogeneity: An Artificial Intelligence Privacy-Utility Bound for Cooperative Data Sharing
items.abstract: Cross-silo crop-yield prediction in computer agriculture requires cooperative learning across farms, cooperatives and extension agencies whose data cannot be pooled because of privacy regulation, commercial sensitivity and heterogeneous sensing regimes. Federated distillation has been proposed as a communication-efficient alternative to federated averaging, but its interaction with formal differential privacy under cross-silo heterogeneity has not been characterised analytically. The analysis decomposes the generalisation gap into three terms: a distillation bias that scales with the disagreement between silo posteriors, a Rényi-differential-privacy noise term that scales with the number of distillation rounds and the privacy budget, and a heterogeneity term that grows with the divergence of silo label distributions. The bound predicts that under high cross-silo heterogeneity the privacy cost of distillation is sub-linear in the number of silos, whereas the utility cost of local-only training is linear in the number of silos, so that distillation dominates local training above a threshold heterogeneity that the bound makes explicit. The bound is illustrated against a random-effects synthesis of country-level associations between electricity access and under-five mortality across 24 African countries (pooled effect -2.19361, standard error 0.26513, 95% CI [-2.71326, -1.67395], I-squared 99.2%), which establishes the order of magnitude of between-silo heterogeneity that the theory must accommodate. The contribution is a formal privacy-utility characterisation that converts a design choice in cooperative agricultural data sharing into a computable threshold.

items.title: Evaluation of first aid guidance for dermal chemical exposure in Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) used in occupational settings
items.abstract: Background Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) are widely used to guide first aid following occupational chemical exposure. However, the clarity and adequacy of SDS recommendations for dermal exposure remain uncertain. Objectives This study evaluated the adequacy and clarity of first aid instructions in sub-section 4.1 of SDSs used in a biotechnology research workplace. Methods First aid instructions in 45 SDSs were assessed against World Health Organization guidelines and peer-reviewed burn management literature. Key criteria included instructions on removal of contaminated clothing and accessories, irrigation procedures (duration of irrigation and source of water), wound care guidance, and recommendations to seek medical attention. Results For chemicals capable of causing dermal burns (Category 1 skin corrosives), only 22% of SDSs recommended immediate removal of contaminated clothing, and 44% advised seeking urgent medical attention after irrigation. Although irrigation was mentioned in all SDSs, essential details such as irrigation duration, use of running water, and the role of emergency showers were omitted. Similar deficiencies were observed for chemicals associated with less severe dermal injuries. Conclusions Many SDSs provide limited and nonspecific first aid guidance for dermal chemical exposure. Insufficient instructions may compromise early response to workplace chemical accidents and increase reliance on emergency medical services. Strengthening SDS guidance, together with enhanced occupational health training and involvement of occupational health professionals in workplace safety programs, may improve preparedness for chemical exposure accidents.

items.title: Evaluation of Gradient-Boosted Propensity-Matching Estimators for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Input-Subsidy Targeting Under District-Level Political Favoritism: A Governance Misallocation-Rate Bound for Smallholder Eligibility
items.abstract: The problem is that machine-learning targeting models are typically evaluated on predictive accuracy, not on the governance-relevant quantity: the rate at which subsidies are misallocated to ineligible households. A replication-based evaluation was conducted using 600 data sets of N = 500 drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). The ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under this process. The estimated bias for the intercept was -0.01261 and for exposure 0.00031; the root mean squared error was 0.84934 for the intercept and 0.01519 for exposure. Empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. A governance misallocation-rate bound can be derived from the sampling distribution of the exposure coefficient, and that this bound is more informative for subsidy targeting than conventional accuracy metrics. The contribution is a methodological framework that connects estimator behaviour to the political-economy problem of district-level favoritism, and a set of propositions about when gradient-boosted matching can be expected to reduce misallocation.

items.title: Evaluation of Mandatory-Human-Review Trigger Calibration for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Pesticide-Advisory Systems Under Regulatory Capture: A Governance Override-Rate Bound for Smallholder Safety
items.abstract: Mandatory human review is the principal safety valve written into proposals for regulating artificial-intelligence pesticide advisory systems in smallholder agriculture, yet the trigger that activates review is almost always specified as a fixed confidence threshold rather than as a governance instrument calibrated to the political economy of the regulator. It treats the override rate — the share of advisory outputs that a calibrated trigger routes to human review — as the object of institutional choice, and derives the conditions under which a trigger chosen by a captured regulator falls below the rate required to protect smallholders. The analysis is theoretical and methodological: no observational data are used or claimed. The bound is expressed as a function of the capture-contingent cost the regulator attaches to overriding industry-preferred advisory outputs, the smallholder safety loss from an unreviewed erroneous recommendation, and the base rate of high-consequence advisories. A trigger calibrated to minimise expected regulatory cost under capture is systematically more permissive than the safety-preserving trigger, and that the gap widens as the capture weight rises. It proposes an override-rate floor as a governance override-rate bound, specifies the audit information needed to enforce it, and identifies the conditions under which the bound is binding. The contribution is a calibration discipline that makes the political vulnerability of the trigger explicit and auditable rather than implicit in a technical threshold.

items.abstract: Temporal-conformal predictors are increasingly proposed as a way to attach distribution-free coverage guarantees to pest-risk forecasts that inform insecticide timing, yet the guarantee is marginal over the calibration window and can fail when the phenology stage of the crop shifts between calibration and deployment. the present analysis treats the coverage guarantee as an auditable object rather than a property to be assumed. It formalises phenology-stage shift as a covariate shift on the stage-conditional risk distribution, derives the conditions under which split-conformal coverage degrades, and proposes a stage-stratified audit that reports coverage per phenology stage rather than in aggregate. The audit is demonstrated on a replication-based evaluation of a linear risk-score estimator with intercept, exposure, group and severity terms, using 600 replications of N = 500 observations drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). The estimator was characterised by ordinary least squares. Estimated bias was -0.01322 for the intercept and 0.00028 for exposure; root-mean-square error was 0.90474 and 0.01575 respectively; empirical coverage of the nominal 95% intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The audit shows that aggregate coverage can be satisfied while stage-conditional coverage is not, and that the gap is a function of the stage-shift magnitude and the calibration-stage composition. The contribution is a coverage-guarantee audit protocol and a formal statement of when temporal-conformal pest-risk forecasts remain safe for insecticide-timing decisions.
